question: What is the most common layer of the uterus where uterine cancer originates?
explanation: The vast majority of uterine malignancies develop from the cells lining the uterine cavity, known as the endometrium. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Why does uterine cancer often have a high cure rate when caught early?

options.A: It is completely resistant to local invasion
options.B: It triggers immediate and severe systemic pain
options.C: It only occurs in younger women with strong immunity
options.D: It produces noticeable symptoms before spreading

explanation: Abnormal vaginal bleeding usually prompts patients to seek medical evaluation before the cancer metastasizes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Which type of cancer makes up the majority of all uterine cancer cases?
explanation: Adenocarcinoma arising from the glandular cells makes up roughly eighty to ninety percent of all uterine cancer diagnoses. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: What makes Type II endometrial cancers different from Type I tumors?

options.A: Type II tumors respond best to mild hormone therapy alone
options.B: Type II tumors are typically high-grade and estrogen-independent
options.C: Type II tumors only occur in patients under forty years old
options.D: Type II tumors never spread outside the muscular wall

explanation: Unlike slow-growing Type I cancers driven by estrogen, Type II tumors are aggressive and unrelated to hormone levels. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: Prolonged exposure to which hormone without progesterone increases uterine cancer risk?
explanation: Unbalanced estrogen stimulation prompts continuous proliferation of the endometrial lining, increasing mutation risks. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: A fifty-five-year-old patient with obesity, hypertension, and no history of pregnancy is being assessed. What condition is she most at risk for developing?
explanation: Obesity converts androgens to estrogen in fatty tissue, creating a high-risk environment for endometrial cell overgrowth in women who have never been pregnant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: What is the most common presenting symptom of uterine cancer in postmenopausal women?
explanation: Any postmenopausal bleeding is considered abnormal and is the primary indicator that triggers diagnostic workup for uterine cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Why is heavy or irregular bleeding in perimenopausal women sometimes ignored by patients?

options.A: It always resolves spontaneously without medical intervention
options.B: It never presents with cramping or pelvic discomfort
options.C: It is universally painless and unaccompanied by fatigue
options.D: It is incorrectly blamed on normal menopausal changes

explanation: Irregular bleeding during perimenopause is often dismissed as normal hormonal shifting, which can unfortunately delay timely cancer diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Which diagnostic procedure gives a definitive tissue diagnosis of uterine cancer?
explanation: Pathological examination of tissue obtained directly from the endometrium is required to confirm malignancy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a transvaginal ultrasound in a patient with bleeding?

options.A: To destroy malignant cells using high-frequency sound
options.B: To measure endometrial thickness and spot abnormalities
options.C: To remove small polyps without surgical incision
options.D: To deliver topical chemotherapy directly to the tumor

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging tool that helps determine whether the endometrial lining is thickened enough to require biopsy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the standard surgical treatment for primary uterine cancer?

options.C: Radical oophorectomy leaving the uterus intact
options.D: Dilation and curettage with local cryotherapy

explanation: Removing the uterus along with both fallopian tubes and ovaries is the standard surgical approach to treat and stage uterine cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: Why might a patient receive radiation or chemotherapy after having a complete hysterectomy?

options.A: To eliminate any remaining microscopic cancer cells and lower recurrence risk
options.B: To stimulate rapid regeneration of the removed pelvic organs
options.C: To prevent the development of unrelated cardiovascular disorders
options.D: To replace lost hormones after surgical removal of the ovaries

explanation: Additional treatments target stray cancer cells that may have spread beyond the primary surgical site, improving long-term survival. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: A patient recovering from a radical hysterectomy shows signs of calf swelling and pain. What complication should the nurse suspect?
explanation: Pelvic surgery and staying in bed for too long increase the risk of blood clot formation in the lower legs, which shows up as calf pain and swelling. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention is most effective for preventing early postoperative pulmonary complications?

options.A: Encouraging deep breathing exercises and early ambulation
options.B: Administering high-dose sedatives to suppress coughing
options.C: Restricting oral fluid intake to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Maintaining strict bedrest until all sutures are removed

explanation: Getting patients moving and expanding their lungs prevents atelectasis and venous stasis after major pelvic surgery. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)
